extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, IP practitioners, government officials, and legal scholars working on GCC/EU intellectual property policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and comparing GCC intellectual property laws and practices (copyright, related/neighboring rights, collective management, trademarks, and geographical indications), including statutory terms, grounds for refusal, procedural rules, and treaty alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: copyright_term_by_work_type
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of copyright protection varies by work type and country (e.g., audiovisual/collective works, anonymous/pseudonymous, applied art, photographs, computer programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from GCC laws: audiovisual or collective works — fifty years after first publication; works published under a pseudonym or anonymously — fifty years after publication; Saudi Arabia: audio, audiovisual works, films, collective works, and computer programs — 50 years from first show or publication; applied art works and photographs — 25 years from publication; UAE: economic rights of applied art works — 25 years after first publication; collective works (except applied arts) and anonymous/pseudonymous works — 50 years after first publication. (References: various national Copyright and Related Rights laws cited in the report.)

rubrics_metrics.name: related_rights_definition_and_treaty_alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Related (neighboring) rights cover performers' rights in performances, producers of sound recordings (phonograms), and broadcasting organizations' rights in their programs, and should align with TRIPS and the WPPT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes that protection is in line with TRIPS and the WPPT; Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE are Rome Convention members; most GCC countries are members or in process of joining WPPT; Qatar and the UAE joined the Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances, which strengthens performers' rights in the audiovisual industry and encourages states to amend national law accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: term_of_protection_for_related_rights_-_bahrain
rubrics_metrics.description: Bahrain: economic rights of performing artists and phonorecord producers protected for seventy years commencing from the beginning of the calendar year following first legal publication; broadcasting corporations’ rights — 20 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If works were published during fifty years from completion, financial protection shall lapse seventy years from the beginning of the calendar year following performance/completion. (See Chapter Seven, Section two of Law No. 22 of 2006 and amendments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: term_of_protection_for_related_rights_-_kuwait
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuwait: performers protected for fifty years after performance or fixation in a phonogram; producers of phonograms protected for fifty years after publication (or after fixation if not published within fifty years); broadcasting organizations' term — twenty years after first broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory formulations distinguish between fixation/publication and performance dates as triggers for the term. (See Chapter 3 of Law No. 75 of 2019.)

rubrics_metrics.name: term_of_protection_for_related_rights_-_oman
rubrics_metrics.description: Oman: economic rights of performers and producers of sound recordings protected for 95 years after the work is legally published for the first time; broadcasting organizations' programs — twenty years after first broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oman's protection terms are notably longer in the report; verify against national legislation for specific triggering events (publication vs fixation).

rubrics_metrics.name: term_of_protection_for_related_rights_-_uae
rubrics_metrics.description: UAE: performers' economic rights protected for fifty years after performance; producers of phonograms — fifty years after publication; broadcasting organizations' rights — twenty years after first transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UAE is amending laws to reflect treaty obligations (e.g., Beijing Treaty), and is in the process of establishing CMOs for literary works as a model. (See national law citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: term_of_protection_for_related_rights_-_saudi_qatar_variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Saudi Arabia and Qatar: performers and producers of recordings generally protected for 50 years from performance/first recording or publication; broadcasting organizations' protection typically 20 years from first transmission/broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saudi provisions state 50 years from date of performance or first recording/publication; broadcasting organizations — 20 years from first transmission. Qatar protects performers until end of fiftieth year following fixation or following performance year if no fixation. (See national law articles cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: collective_management_organization_(CMO)_role_and_framework
rubrics_metrics.description: CMOs are important to help right holders collect rights and improve enforcement; legal frameworks may allow authors to grant exclusive licenses to professional societies to manage economic rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report highlights that Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and the UAE included CMO provisions in law but few CMOs are operational due to lack of implementing regulations; implementing regulations and ministry supervision (licensing, fees, control) are necessary for CMOs to operate. The UAE plans a licensed 'Reproduction Centre for Books and Literary Works' as an initial CMO model. Capacity-building (workshops, study visits, internships) and adaptation to social/economic context are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: trademark_definition_and_scope_of_what_counts_as_a_mark
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory definition of a trademark varies but generally covers signs that distinguish goods/services — names, words, signatures, letters, designs, logos, colors (including single non-functional colors), sounds and scents, packaging and shapes; some laws explicitly include voice/odor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country examples: GCC Trademark Law: 'anything having a distinctive form such as names, words, signatures, letters, figures, drawings, logos... The voice or odor shall be considered as part of the trademark.' Oman/Qatar/UAE formulations expand to include holograms, geographical indications, sounds, scents and tastes in some texts. Non-traditional marks like tastes, holograms and motion marks may not be covered uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiclass_filing_and_classification_practices
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC Trademark Law allows filing multiclass applications; however, the UAE has historically required single-class applications (a practice to be changed under new law). All GCC countries use the Nice Classification (membership varies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bahrain and Oman are members of the Nice Agreement; Kuwait/Qatar/Saudi may exclude certain classes (e.g., alcoholic beverages, pork-related classes) via implementing regulations. Harmonization (e.g., adopting Madrid/Singapore Treaty provisions) is recommended to eliminate single-class constraints and onerous document legalization requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: grounds_for_refusal_of_trademark_registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Common statutory grounds: lack of distinctiveness; contrary to public order or morality; official/state emblems or flags; religious symbols; geographical names that create confusion about origin; marks identical or confusingly similar to earlier or well-known marks; marks misleading the public; use of protected words (e.g., 'Registered', 'Copyright').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws provide for refusal when marks are identical/confusingly similar to well-known marks even if unregistered; additional prohibitions include names/logos of third parties without consent, marks that mislead on nature/quality/origin, and special categories per national laws. Specific lists and examples vary by country (see Table 9 and national law citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: well-known_mark_protection_criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of a well-known mark may consider public awareness, promotions, long period of registration or use, number of countries where registered or renowned, the value of the trademark, and its effect on promoting goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-known trademark may not be registered in the GCC unless the owner or representative requests registration. Protection can extend beyond identical/similar goods where use would indicate a link or prejudice the renowned owner's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: non-use_cancellation_periods_and_definition_of_use
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registrations can be cancelled for non-use: commonly five consecutive years (Bahrain/Kuwait/Saudi/UAE/Qatar), but Oman provides three consecutive years or longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks may be removed if not seriously used during the statutory period unless special circumstances (import restrictions, government impediments) justify non-use. The GCC laws generally lack clear statutory definitions of 'use'; the report recommends following EU Directive 2015/2436 which lists examples constituting use (use in an equivalent form not altering distinctiveness; affixing to goods/packaging solely for export).

rubrics_metrics.name: trademark_term_renewal_and_grace_periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks are protected for ten years in GCC countries and renewable indefinitely for additional ten-year periods upon renewal and fee payment; grace periods for maintenance fees differ (Paris Convention: six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UAE historically applied a three-month grace period for maintenance fee payment (contradicting the Paris Convention's six-month grace), an incompatibility to be addressed in the new UAE Trademark Law which will adopt a six-month period. Ministries may notify owners of expiry per national practice (UAE informs owner the month following expiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: procedural_requirements_affecting_registration_quality_and_priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules — notarization/legalization of foreign documents, substantive and formal examinations, opposition procedures — impact cost, delay, and claim to priority for trademark applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report criticizes current systems as costly and time-consuming due to notarization/legalization requirements for foreign trademarks, which frequently cause missed priority dates. It also notes variable quality of substantive examination and recommends capacity building for examiners and adoption of international procedural treaties (Madrid Protocol, Trademark Law Treaty, Singapore Treaty) to modernize systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: geographical_indications_definition_and_protection_models
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs identify goods as originating in a territory/region/locality where a quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. Protection models in GCC vary: sui generis systems (Bahrain, Qatar, Oman) vs protection as certification or collective marks under the Unified Trademark Law (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of protection includes agricultural and non-agricultural products, including handicrafts. Laws of GCC countries that provide sui generis systems mirror TRIPS definitions; countries using the Unified Trademark Law may not define GIs explicitly. Oman is in the final phase of adhering to the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement; all GCC members are WTO members and bound by TRIPS Articles 22–24 on GIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: international_treaty_adherence_and_implementation_recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to international IP treaties (TRIPS, Paris Convention, Rome Convention, WPPT, Beijing Treaty, Madrid Protocol, TLT, Singapore Treaty) affects domestic rights and procedural standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes uneven treaty membership across GCC countries (e.g., Bahrain/Oman members of Madrid Protocol and TLT; Qatar/UAE recently joined Beijing Treaty). It recommends accession/adherence to instruments like the Singapore Treaty, Madrid Protocol, and alignment with EU Directive 2015/2436 to harmonize procedures, modernize classification usage, eliminate onerous requirements (single-class, notarization), and clarify definitions such as 'use' for non-use cancellation.
